summary: I approve. The holder-scoped release is correct. Both insertClaimed and reclaimProvision RETURNING the provision_claimed_at they wrote. The column is timestamptz with microsecond storage. pgjdbc reads it with getObject(OffsetDateTime) and binds it back with setObject(OffsetDateTime) at microsecond precision, so the compare-and-release is exact and does not depend on a Java clock. now() is evaluated on the DB side for both the write and the compare. PaymentService is not @Transactional, so each statement autocommits with its own now() and the lease is visible to other callers straight away. A release cannot clear another holder's lease. A takeover only succeeds when the old stamp is NULL or older than now() minus the lease, so a takeover stamp is always later than the one it replaces. Equality with a stale holder's token would need the DB clock to step backwards at exactly the wrong microsecond, and even then the stale holder releases only once. A release racing a reclaim is serialised by the row lock. Under READ COMMITTED the loser re-checks the updated row: a late release sees the new stamp and matches 0 rows, and a late reclaim sees NULL and takes the lease. A holder always clears its own lease unless provider_order_id has already been set, and then there is nothing to release. In every failure mode the worst outcome is still an orphan Razorpay order. The conditional publish (provider_order_id IS NULL, plus the mode, status and method guard) still stores at most one payable id. The original exception is kept: the release runs in its own try/catch, a release failure is attached with e.addSuppressed, and the Razorpay exception is rethrown. The comment now says that a timeout counts as a failure and that an orphan is the accepted worst case, which matches CTO ruling items 1-4. Nothing new is introduced: no endpoints, auth changes, dependencies, string-built SQL (all values are bound parameters), or secrets or PII in logs. Two tests were added: the stale-release takeover and the mode-switch publish guard. The PaymentPropertiesValidationTest move is a pure rename and has no security impact. Its package declaration presumably still says `service` while the file now sits in the config directory, so code review may want to tidy that. The one open item is the round-2 V8 checksum minor. It has not been written up as a PR note yet, so I carry it as a minor to record in the PR description.
